name: Me'paa de Acatepec

catalog_quote: Los Tonos. La presentación de los tonos a continuación presume la presencia de melodías tonales en algunos temas simples. Todas las posibilidades de melodías consistiendo de uno o dos tonos parecen ser bien atestiguadas en los temas con dos sílabas. ... [Melodía: Bajo, Medio, Alto, Bajo-Medio, Bajo-Alto, Medio-Bajo, Medio-Alto, Alto-Bajo, Alto-Medio] ... La Prominencia Silábica. Marlett y Weathers (en preparación) argumentan que las lenguas me phaa generalmente tienen una estructura yámbica, aunque nada precisamente de carácter como "acento" se ha identificado. La última sílaba es más fuerte que las otras, que es un tipo de prominencia. Esta prominencia se refleja en los detalles fonéticos de las consonantes, los cuales se discuten en la sección Convenciones.

new_statements.quote: Tlapanec employs iambic feet aligned to the right edge of the prosodic word (Marlett and Weathers 2018: 23; Suárez 1983: 26). The acoustic correlate of accent in Tlapanec is still unclear. On the one hand, Marlett and Weathers (2018: 23) state that “it is not clear that something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Me’phaa”; and speakers also have difficulty in identifying which syllable is ‘strong’. […] Marlett and Weathers (2018: 23–24) remark that there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed (whether this syllable has a short vowel or long vowel; thus, quantity-insensitive), since various phonological and phonetic details require reference to a weak syllable of the foot.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Me'paa de Acatepec has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work supplies a placement (final syllable of the prosodic word, quantity-insensitive, iterative iambs with secondary accent) together with the explicit caveat that the phonetic status of stress is disputed. Caveat on identity: all data are from the Huehuetepec variety (Zilacayotitlán), which Marlett's survey (held by the project) groups under Malinaltepec Me'phaa [tcf] ('tlapaneco del este'), not Acatepec [tpx]; but the prosodic claim is stated for Tlapanec as a whole via Marlett & Weathers 2018 and Suárez 1983, and Cline 2013: 51 (Acatepec variety, already held by the project) reports the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The prosodic word is right-headed: its last syllable is the 'strong' (accented) syllable, head of a right-aligned iambic foot, regardless of vowel length (quantity-insensitive). The language is tonal (three level tones L/M/H on moras, p. 87), and the authors deliberately say 'strong/weak' rather than 'stressed/unstressed' because the phonetic correlate of stress is unsettled: Marlett & Weathers (2018) doubt that anything comparable to stress is identifiable, Carrasco Zúñiga (2012) proposes onset-consonant duration in the strong syllable as the correlate (the authors' own impression supports this), and Herrera Zendejas (2018) claims accent goes to the syllable with the right-most highest tone. Phonological correlates of the final strong syllable: vowel length, nasalization and contour tones are contrastive only there; it alone resists syncope; it requires an onset more strictly (pp. 88–89).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Tlapanec has been argued to employ quantity-insensitive iambic feet and aligns them at the right edge of the prosodic word, assigned iteratively from right to left (cf. Marlett and Weathers 2018).. the strong syllable is indicated with a raised vertical line, while secondary accent is indicated with a lowered vertical line' (p. 100; example (19) is vector-drawn and did not extract). Secondary accent thus falls on the head of each non-final iamb, alternating leftward from the final syllable. Fn. 13: right-to-left and quantity-insensitive iambs are both typologically rare.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounded roots are not counted in the syllable count and compounds may not form one prosodic word (fn. 14, p. 100); a few contour tones occur in non-final syllables (p. 87); [d] occasionally appears in weak syllables in loans and compounds (p. 87). Speakers have difficulty identifying the strong syllable (p. 88).
new_statements.identity_note: Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano 2021 describe the Huehuetepec variety (Zilacayotitlán, Atlamajalcingo del Monte; the second author's native variety), which INALI calls 'tlapaneco del este' and which Marlett's survey (held by the project:, table p. 3) places under Malinaltepec Me'phaa [tcf] rather than Acatepec [tpx] = acat1239. The prosodic statements quoted are nonetheless framed for Tlapanec generally and rest on Marlett & Weathers 2018 and Suárez 1983; Cline 2013 (Acatepec Me'paa, p. 51 '1.4.4 Prominence') gives the same right-headed/iambic, 'no clear evidence of stress' description for all varieties.

readall_conflicts: Within the one opened work there is an explicit disagreement among the cited sources on whether Tlapanec has stress at all and what its correlate is: Marlett & Weathers (2018: 23) say 'it is not clear that something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Me'phaa' (and speakers cannot readily pick the strong syllable), Carrasco Zúñiga (2012) takes onset-consonant duration in the final strong syllable as the correlate, and Herrera Zendejas (2018) assigns accent to the syllable bearing the right-most highest tone, which would make placement tone-dependent rather than fixed: final syllable. Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano side with a right-headed, quantity-insensitive, iambic analysis (final syllable strong) but leave the acoustic question open. Cline 2013: 51 (Acatepec variety, held by the project from the earlier reading) states the same Marlett & Weathers position: no clear evidence of stress, but right-headed iambic structure in all varieties. So the placement (final) is uncontested among these; whether it is 'stress' is.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation and the domain quotation are verbatim in the PDF we hold (decoded text), with one locator slip: 'Los Tonos'/'La Prominencia Silábica' are on p.6, not p.7 (Roticización p.8 is right), and the item is 11 pp, not 8. (2) The source is a 2012 JIPA-style phonetic illustration by Marlett, the main Me'phaa phonologist, with a native-speaker co-author - short and 'preliminary' but first-hand and variety-specific. (3) The one clearly better work in Glottolog's list, Cline 2013 (UND MA thesis on the tone system of this exact variety, 215 pp), was not yet obtained; it is now downloaded from an Internet Archive copy of UND Scholarly Commons and read: sect. 1.4.4 'Prominence' (pp. 51-52) repeats the position verbatim in substance - 'no clear evidence of something like stress in Me'phaa', 'right-headed, or iambic, prosodic structure', word-final syllables strong / non-final weak, /d/ -> [r] in w

sources.quote: p.51: 'Marlett and Weathers propose that, while there is no clear evidence of something like stress in Meꞌphaa, words and phrases in all varieties demonstrate a right-headed, or iambic, prosodic structure (in preparation:24). Some phonetic details depend on references to a weak syllable. For example, in major class words, the phoneme /d/ is consistently pronounced as [d] when it occurs in the final, strong syllable of disyllabic words ... When it occurs in non-final, weak syllables ... it is pronounced as [r].' fn.5: 'Word-final syllables are strong, while non-final syllables are weak.' p.13:
sources.locator: sect. 1.4.4 'Prominence', pp. 51-52; sect. 1.3.1 p. 13 (three contrastive tone heights); fn. 5 (word-final syllables strong); fn. 9 p. 24; abstract (all nine two-tone melodies on disyllabic nouns)
